newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia-Australia forum to focus on economics.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia-Australia forum to focus on economics.

text.p: Australia and Indonesia are expected to focus on economics rather than thorny political issues during a two-day ministerial forum opening on Thursday.

The third annual Indonesia-Australia ministerial forum will also give the new conservative government in Canberra an opportunity to establish its credentials with its northern neighbour, the world's fourth most populous nation.
The seven-member Australian delegation covers the trade, foreign affairs, education, industry, health, transport and environment ministries.

"The discussions will be mostly on economic issues but the meeting has symbolic political importance," Ikrar Nusa Bhakti, a senior researcher at the Jakarta Centre for Political and Regional Studies, told Reuters.
"This shows that the new Australian government will not change the previous government's policy of strengthening the Australia-Indonesia relationship," Bhakti said.
"This forum is second in importance only to meetings between the president and prime minister," he added.

The Australian delegation includes Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer and Foreign Minister Alexander Downer, both on their third visit to Indonesia since their conservative coalition government took office last March.
Downer said in a statement earlier this week that the forum was established to expand the bilateral relationship in the areas of practical economic and trade cooperation.

He is also due to have a separate meeting with Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas. Officials from both sides said they expected bilateral and regional political issues to be discussed during this meeting.

These could include East Timor and Indonesia's attitude after the 1996 Nobel peace prize was jointly awarded to East Timorese Bishop Carlos Belo and self-exiled Timorese resistance spokesman Jose Ramos Horta, who lives in Australia.
"East Timor will not be discussed in the forum but it will probably be discussed at the bilateral (foreign ministers' meeting)," an Australian official said.
Indonesia invaded East Timor, a former Portuguese colony, in 1975 and annexed the territory the following year, a move never recognised by the United Nations.
Australia's conservative government has been attacked by its opponents who say Canberra has focused on ties with traditional Western allies at the expense of Asian neighbours.

Former Labor prime minister Paul Keating had been known for his close friendship with Indonesian President Suharto which political analysts say allowed the two countries to sign a landmark security agreement last December.

"This year's meeting will provide the government with the opportunity to underline the importance that Australia attaches to promoting trade, investment and general business links with Indonesia," Downer said.
He said the forum was a vehicle to address impediments to trade and investment as well as provide an opportunity to explore likely future directions and growth areas in our economies.
The visiting Australian ministers will sign or witness the signing of a number of government and private sector cooperation agreements across all the participating sectors.

Bhakti said participation by Australian companies in an Indonesian government project to design a local car, known as the Maleo, was likely to be discussed, as well as the sale of Indonesian commercial and military aircraft in Australia.
